title.en: How the Hare Got His Split Lip

region.en: High mountain road above a Tibetan valley (symbolic pin in the Changtang highlands)
region.zh: 藏北高原山路（以羌塘高地為象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story I

summary.en: A Tiger catches a Hare, who talks him into eating his own eyes on the promise they grow again, then leads the blind Tiger to a fire at the edge of a gulf until he falls; trapped on a tree-bough by his teeth, the Tiger is talked into saying 'Ah!' and dashed to the rocks. Next day the Hare engineers a whole morning of catastrophe - horses stampeded by ravens, sheep scattered by a wolf, a man skinning the dead Tiger - and watches it all from a hilltop, laughing until his upper lip splits, which it has remained ever since.
summary.zh: 虎捕兔，兔哄虎吃掉自己的雙眼（說會再生），再把失明的虎引到懸崖邊烤火，跌落深谷；虎齒咬住樹枝懸空，兔哄牠開口喊「啊」，虎便墜石而死。次日兔又接連撮合——烏鴉啄馬、狼逐羊、人剝虎皮——自己立於山頂旁觀，笑得前唇豁裂，至今如此。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected during a British diplomatic mission to Tibet (1906); treated respectfully as heritage of the Tibetan storytelling tradition.

passages.text: As they went along night began to fall, and when it was quite dark the Hare began smacking his chops as if he was eating something very nice. 'I am eating my eye, Uncle Tiger,' he replied; 'it is very nice, and it soon grows again.' The hungry Tiger scraped out his own eye and ate it; a little further on the Hare ate his other eye 'even better than the first', and the Tiger, quite blind, was led to the brink of a deep gulf and advised to sit down and rest while a fire was lighted in front of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the blazing sticks came nearer the Tiger edged further and further back until he toppled over backwards into the gulf - and half-way down he seized a bough growing from a cleft with his teeth. Peeping over the edge, the Hare called out that he was afraid the Tiger must be badly hurt, and asked him to just say 'Ah!' so that he would know he was all right; the Tiger opened his mouth to say it and was instantly precipitated to the bottom, where he fell upon some rocks and was killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning the Hare offered a horse-driver the dead Tiger's skin, and while he skinned it set two Ravens to peck the sores on his unguarded horses; then he offered a shepherd-boy a raven's nest full of eggs, and while he climbed for them invited a Wolf down upon the unguarded sheep. From the top of a high hill the Hare surveyed the whole morning's work - the man stripping the Tiger, the horses careering with the ravens, the boy robbing the nest, the sheep scattered to the four quarters - and, leaning back on a stone, laughed so much that he split his upper lip, which has remained split to this very day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tiger and the Man: The Dying Father's Warning

region.en: Jungle edge of a Tibetan valley (symbolic pin in the Kham hills)
region.zh: 康區山谷林緣（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story II

summary.en: A dying Father Tiger warns his three cubs that of all animals only Man is more powerful and cunning than the Tiger, and must never be hunted. The elder brothers obey; the youngest, proud of his stripes and claws, sets out to prove otherwise - and is lectured in turn by a scarred old Bullock and a goad-scarred old Elephant, both of whom Man served while strong and discarded when old. He finally meets the Woodcutter, who demonstrates the house - and when the boastful Tiger demands it, walks off locking him in to starve.
summary.zh: 臨終的虎父告誡三子：世間唯「人」比虎更強更狡，切不可獵。兩位兄長謹遵父命；幼虎仗著利爪斑紋，偏要證明父親錯了——路上先聽盡老牛與老象的控訴（年輕力壯時受寵，衰老即遭拋棄），最後遇見樵夫。樵夫演示了「房子」的妙處；幼虎強索此屋，被反鎖屋內活活餓死。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: Remember, my children, said the dying Father Tiger, that the Tiger is Lord of the jungle; but there is one animal against whom you must be on your guard, for he alone is more powerful and cunning than the Tiger. That animal is Man - I warn you solemnly before I die to beware of Man, and on no account to try to hunt or to kill him. The elder brothers confined themselves to deer and pigs; the youngest, of an independent and inquisitive disposition, chafed at the restriction.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: A worn-out pack-Bullock warned him with his own scars: while I was young and strong he cared for me, but as soon as I became old and weak and unable to do his work he turned me out to the jungle and gave no thought for me in my old age. An ancient Elephant said the same: Man made me his servant, put a saddle on my back and made stirrups of my ears, and used to strike me over the head with an iron goad - leave Man alone, or it will be the worse for you in the end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Woodcutter, asked what sort of animal he was, showed the Tiger his timber house: you poor animals live in a hole in the forest exposed to wind, rain, cold and heat, while I build myself a fine house indifferent to the weather. The conceited Tiger flew into a passion - I am far more worthy than you of a house, come out at once and give it to me - and stalked in; the Man bolted the door outside and walked off with his axe, leaving the Tiger to starve to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

region.en: Woodcutter's hut in a Tibetan forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 藏地林中樵夫小屋（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story III

summary.en: Trapped in the Woodcutter's hut, a starving Tiger promises a Musk Deer freedom if she unbolts the door - then seizes her, denying there is any such thing as good faith. They agree to refer the question to the first three living things they meet: the roadside Tree reports travellers who break his branches for whips; the Buffalo reports a calf that pushes its mother from the best pasture; the Hare, third judge, pleads ignorance of the story's details and walks the two back to the hut to demonstrate - where the Tiger shows how it was done, and the door is bolted on him for good.
summary.zh: 被困小屋的餓虎請麝鹿開門並許諾放生——出門即咬住她，還說世上根本沒有「信義」。雙方約定請三個活物評理：路邊大樹說旅人折其枝作鞭；水牛說牛犢長大便把母親趕出好草地；第三位裁判兔子裝糊塗，請二人回小屋現場演說——虎進屋演示，兔子與麝鹿把門栓上揚長而去，虎不久餓死屋中。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: When the Tiger seized the Deer and said he had no alternative but to eat her, she reproached him for breaking his faith, and he answered: Faith! I don't believe there is any such thing as good faith. So they made a bargain to ask the first three living things they met; the Tree, consulted first, gave shelter to man and beast on the highway and got broken branches for whips in return - my experience leads me to believe that there is no such thing as good faith in this world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old Cow Buffalo, who stinted herself so her calf might have the best of everything, chewed the cud and gave the same verdict: as soon as the calf is big enough it will push me away from the places where I am grazing and drive me altogether from the pastures - my experience makes me believe there is no such thing as good faith. Downhearted, the Deer begged one more chance, the third and last judge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Hare, hearing the strange story, professed himself unable to follow exactly who was shut up where, and proposed that all three adjourn to the scene of action. At the hut he had the Deer take her place at the stream and the Tiger take his inside; then, remarking that the door must have been shut like so, he shut it and bolted it, and he and the Deer went on their way safely, leaving the Tiger inside, where he shortly afterwards starved to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Neighbours: Chamba and Tsering

region.en: Two houses side by side in a Tibetan village (symbolic pin in the Tsangpo valley)
region.zh: 藏南雅魯藏布谷地某村的兩戶人家（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story IV

summary.en: The generous poor man Chamba binds up a fallen sparrow's broken leg - the bird is a fairy in disguise - and is repaid with a grain that grows into jewel-bearing ears; the proud rich man Tsering drops a sparrow with chopsticks to manufacture the same luck, and his grain grows into a creditor apparition from a former existence, who seizes his whole property and makes him a slave. Reduced to want, Tsering embezzles the gold-dust his neighbour entrusts to him and refills the bag with sand - 'it has turned into this!' - and Chamba pays him back with a schooled monkey who cries 'worthy father, I am turned into this!' until the thief restores the gold to recover his own son.
summary.zh: 善良窮人強巴為摔傷的麻雀綁好斷腿（小鳥實為仙人化身），得珠粒為報；傲慢富人次仁用筷子把小麻雀摔下人造「善緣」，種出的卻是前世債主，被奪全部家產淪為奴僕。窮途末路的次仁又侵吞鄰人寄存的金沙、以沙充數，一句「變成這樣了！」——強巴便以一隻訓練過的猴子回敬「父親大人，我變成這樣了！」，直至他賠出金沙才領回親兒。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The poor man bound up the young Sparrow's broken leg with thread and put it back in the nest; this Sparrow, although the poor man did not know it, was really a fairy in disguise, and when grown it flew in with its beak full of grain: this grain is in return for your kindness - plant it in your garden and see what comes up. The ears of corn contained valuable jewels instead of grain, and the poor man sold them for a large sum and found himself in comfort and prosperity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The rich man picked a young Sparrow out of the nest with a pair of chop-sticks and dropped it, bound up its leg, and got the same grain from a grateful-looking sparrow; but when he planted it in the richest part of his soil, there arose instead of barley a great fierce-looking man with a bundle of papers under his arm: I was a creditor of yours in one of your former existences. He seized the rich man's house, cattle, sheep and lands, and reduced him to a slave in his own household.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Entrusted with a bag of gold-dust, the impoverished Tsering spent it all and filled the bag with sand; Chamba, opening it, found sand instead of gold, and the dishonest neighbour could only say: my friend, it has turned into this! Then Chamba announced a free school for little boys, and while Tsering was away procured a tame Monkey taught to say 'worthy father, I am turned into this!' When the father demanded his son, the monkey repeated the words, and he decided it was better to pay up the stolen gold on condition of having his proper son restored.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cat and the Mice: The Procession Trick

region.en: Great farm-house of a Tibetan village (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 藏地某村大農舍（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story V

summary.en: A Cat too old to hunt announces her repentance and asks the mice only to file past her twice daily in obeisance - and devours the last mouse of every procession. The two clever friends Rambe and Ambe counter with a roll-call: one always leads and one always trails, calling back and forth until all have passed. When at last the furious Cat leaps into the middle of the column, the warned mice scuttle to their holes, the room stands empty, and the Cat soon dies of starvation.
summary.zh: 老貓捕鼠無力，宣稱已悔過向善，只求鼠群一日兩次列隊打恭——隊尾的最後一隻總是被她吃掉。聰明的朋友然巴與安巴識破，以點名法破解：一隻永在隊首、一隻永在隊尾，一路互相唱和直至全體通過。老貓忍無可忍撲向隊伍中央，早有防備的鼠群四散入洞，房中頓空；老貓不久餓死。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: I have led a very wicked life, said the Cat to the assembled mice, and in my old age I repent; henceforth I shall give myself up to religious contemplation and no longer molest you - all I ask is that twice every day you file past me and each make an obeisance as a token of your gratitude. She took her seat on a cushion, the mice went by in single file, and as soon as the procession had passed with the exception of one little mouse she seized the last one and devoured it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two friends agreed that Rambe was always to walk at the very front and Ambe bring up the rear, calling and answering at frequent intervals: Where are you, Brother Ambe? - Here I am, Brother Rambe. Twice the Cat dared not touch Ambe while his brother kept calling; the third evening she made a fierce leap right into the middle of the mice, who, thoroughly prepared, scuttled off in every direction, and before she could catch a single one the room was empty. After this the mice put no further trust in the treacherous Cat, who soon died of starvation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Foolish Young Mussulman: Grave, Jar and Shadow
title.zh: 糊塗回教青年：掘墓、油罐與樹影

region.en: Meadows and roads outside a large Tibetan trading town (symbolic pin at Gyantse)
region.zh: 藏地大商鎮郊野（以江孜為象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story VI

summary.en: A simple young Mussulman is told that yellow soles mean he will die at once; he digs himself a shallow grave and lies down in it - and is recruited by a passing servant to carry the King's jar of oil for the price of a hen. Dreaming out the hen's eggs, the chickens, the cow, the house, the wife and the child's education, he stamps his foot at the naughty child and smashes the royal jar. Sent to his wedding through a shaded road, he hides his clothes to escape a pursuing shadow, climbs a poplar, and with one shout of 'I want my share too!' scares a caravan of thieves into leaving everything - a horse and garments - below.
summary.zh: 天真的回教青年聽信「腳底發黃必死」之言，自掘淺墓躺進等死；被王之僕半僱半哄背起御用油罐，換得「一隻母雞」的許諾。他一路盤算雞生蛋、蛋變雞、雞換牛、牛換屋、娶妻生子、管教兒子——想到要跺腳教訓，腳下一跺，油罐落地粉碎。成親路上他把衣衫脫下藏好以躲影子，爬上楊樹瞌睡；醒來一聲「我也要分一份！」嚇得路上那夥強人拋下馬匹衣物抱頭而逃。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The soles of your feet are all yellow, called out a passing young man, and that is a sure sign you are going to die at once. The poor fellow dug himself a shallow grave and lay down in it to wait for death, and a King's Servant, passing with a jar of oil, recruited him for a hen; on the road he built up in his head the hen's eggs, the chickens, the cow and calf, the house, the wife and the child's education, and stamped his foot at the naughty imaginary child so violently that the jar of oil slipped off his back and was smashed to pieces on the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sent off to his bride's wedding-feast, he was plagued on a shaded road by a shadow on whichever side he looked, so he stripped off his garments and hung them along the road, climbed into the upper branches of a poplar and fell asleep. A party of travellers collected the scattered garments and the grazing horse and stopped in the tree's shade to divide the spoil - and when the Boy woke and called out 'I want my share too!' they took him for a demon in the tree and fled, leaving the horse and all the clothes behind them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the wedding feast he saved dainties for his mother in a narrow-mouthed copper vessel and got his hand stuck fast in its neck; unable to eat, he was coaxed into telling his bride, who sent him down in the dark to beat the vessel against the white stone at the foot of the stairs - and he struck instead the grey head of his bride's father, asleep there from the feast. Terrified, he fled, slept on a honeycomb and then in a wool-shed, and waking white and woolly believed he had been turned into a sheep as punishment for killing his father-in-law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sheep in the Robbers' Hands and the Cat with the Lantern
title.zh: 強盜背上的「羊」與提燈的貓

region.en: Sheep-fold and inn on the road to India (symbolic pin at Phari)
region.zh: 通往印度的帕里羊圈與客棧（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story VI (continued)

summary.en: Believing himself a sheep, the honey-and-wool-covered youth joins a flock, and at midnight robbers pick him as the fattest; hoisted onto a back and laid down to have his throat cut, he breaks role and cries out, scaring them away. Later, trading to India, he is cheated of everything by an innkeeper who wins a bet that a cat will carry in the lantern at dusk - until his wife, disguised as a man, repeats the wager and has her husband release three mice in the courtyard: the trained cat drops the lantern at the third, the innkeeper loses house and goods, and the couple return home wealthy.
summary.zh: 塗滿蜂蜜羊毛的他自認變成了羊，混入羊群；夜裡強盜挑中他這「最肥的羊」，正要割喉，他忘了角色喊出人話，強盜抱頭而逃。後來他去印度經商，被店主以「貓能提燈」的賭局騙光全部財物——他的妻子扮作男商重下同樣賭注，再讓丈夫在院中連放三隻老鼠：訓練有素的貓在第三隻時丟下燈籠撲鼠，店主輸掉家業連同先前贏的財物，夫婦滿載而歸。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: At midnight robbers came to the fold and felt about for a good fat heavy one, finding the Boy the heaviest of them all; hoisted onto a back and laid on the ground to have his throat cut, this trial proved too much for his nerves, and forgetting his role of sheep he called out in a shrill voice: please don't kill me, kind robbers! They fled as fast as they could, and he returned to his bride's house, where the sorely hurt but not dead father-in-law freely forgave him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: At a large house on the way to India the Landlord bet that when night fell a lantern would be carried into the room by a cat instead of by a servant - a regular trick, for the tame cat carried in a lighted lantern at dusk every evening, by which he secured unwary travellers' goods. The young Man forfeited all he possessed and stayed on as a servant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: His wife, disguised as a man with ponies laden with wool, repeated the wager, and privately told her Husband what he was to do: catch three mice and conceal them in a little box. At dusk, as the cat crossed the courtyard with the lantern in its mouth, one mouse, then a second, then a third were released - and at the third the cat dropped the lantern on the threshold and bounded after the mouse. The Landlord reluctantly owned his bet lost, and handed over not only his own property but the merchandise previously won from her Husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Kyang, the Fox, the Wolf and the Hare

region.en: Upper Tibetan valley beyond cultivation (symbolic pin in the Changtang highlands)
region.zh: 藏地高寒無耕作的河谷上段（以羌塘為象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story VII

summary.en: A young Kyang, too thin for a hungry Wolf, bargains for six months; in autumn the Wolf comes with a Fox and a Hare invited to share the spoil. The Hare proposes strangling the fat Kyang by rope instead of throat-biting, borrows a rope from a shepherd, rigs a big slip-knot for the Kyang and two smaller ones for the Wolf and Fox - and at the word 'pull' the Kyang simply walks forward, dragging his executioners, and gallops off; the two strangle themselves and the Hare trots home feeling he has done a good day's work.
summary.zh: 小野驢以「秋天再肥」哄走餓狼；秋日狼帶著狐與兔同來赴約分贓。兔獻策改咬喉為勒斃，向牧人借繩——大繩圈套野驢頸，狼與狐各把頭伸進兩個小繩圈，兔咬繩尾喊「拉」；野驢向前一走，拖著狼狐便跑，二獸自勒而死，野驢甩繩悠然吃草，兔自覺做了件好事。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: In spring the Kyang told the Wolf it was no good eating him then, thin after the hard winter, but that in autumn he would be twice as fat; the Wolf agreed to wait on condition that they meet on this very spot. In autumn he started for the appointment, picked up the Fox and the Hare to share the spoil, and found the Kyang very fat and sleek, licking his chops in anticipation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Hare suggested that strangling would save the blood a throat-seizure would waste, borrowed a rope from a shepherd's encampment, and rigged it: a large slip-knot over the Kyang's neck, two smaller loops for the heads of the Wolf and the Fox, himself holding the loose end with his teeth. At the word 'pull' the Kyang walked forward a few paces, the rope tightened on the executioners' necks, and when the Hare let go the Kyang galloped off dragging the Wolf and the Fox after him until both were strangled; the Hare scampered home feeling he had done a good day's work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

region.en: House roof and well in a Tibetan village (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 藏地村中屋頂與水井（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story VIII

summary.en: A Crow carries off a fat Frog to devour him on a roof; the Frog chuckles that his fierce Father lives on this very roof, then that a stronger Uncle lives in the gutter, until the Crow retreats to the ground. There the Frog admires her blunt bill and sends her to sharpen it on a flat stone - and dives into the well. Invited down to eat him there, the Crow's own advice traps her: 'the best thing would be for you to come down here.'
summary.zh: 鴉叼著肥蛙上屋頂欲食；蛙先笑言「猛父就住在這屋頂」，再言「更猛的叔父住在水槽」，鴉步步後退下到地面。蛙又贊其喙太鈍，勸牠去磨石上磨利；鴉一轉身，蛙跳井而逃。井邊鴉喚蛙上來受死，蛙答「我上不去，還是請你下來吃我吧」。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: As she alighted the Frog gave an audible chuckle: my Father lives close by here, on this very roof, and he is an exceedingly fierce, strong man who will certainly avenge my death. The Crow hopped to another corner; the Frog chuckled again that his Uncle, even stronger than his Father, lived in the very gutter; and the Crow, alarmed, flew down to the ground near the edge of a well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: There the Frog observed that her bill seemed rather blunt, and advised her to strop it on a flat stone over there before beginning to eat; as soon as her back was turned the Frog gave one desperate jump and dived into the well. When the sharp-billed Crow called down for him to come up and be eaten, he replied that he could not get up the sides of this well - the best thing would be for you to come down here to eat me - and dived to the bottom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

region.en: Rocky den and stone tank on a Tibetan mountainside (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 藏地山腰石穴與石砌水池（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story IX

summary.en: A Hare caught by a Lion offers him a bigger meal: a fierce animal living in the valley pond. The Lion's own reflection, flattered and goaded by the Hare's running commentary, is attacked with a roar - and the masonry-sided tank drowns him. The Hare then boasts to the grieving Lioness that he gave her lord a free fight and left him dying in the valley, leads her at full gallop through the big end of a tapered hole in a ruined wall - and she wedges fast, to be pelted with stones until she starves.
summary.zh: 兔被獅擒，獻上「谷中水池中更強的猛獸」為食；獅向水面自己倒影狂吼撲擊，落入四壁光滑的石池溺斃。兔又對悲傷的母獅自誇「與你家老爺打了一架，他正垂死谷中」，引她狂追鑽入廢牆大口小尾的斜孔——母獅卡死其中，被兔投石辱罵，終至餓斃。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Hare begged the indignant Lion to be careful, promising an animal in the pond stronger than himself; at the square-built stone tank the Lion stalked to the edge and saw his own head reflected. Encouraged by the Hare to keep growling but on no account come to grips with the beast, he was goaded to desperation, sprang straight at the image, and being unable to climb the masonry sides, swam until, quite wearied out, he sank to the bottom and was drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning the Hare told the perturbed Lioness that he and her lord had had a little argument and a free fight, and that he had been obliged to injure Mr. Lion rather severely before making him see reason; as she sprang at him he galloped off, made straight for the ruined wall, entered the breach at the large end and emerged at the small recess. The Lioness, blind with rage, rushed head-foremost into the opening and was wedged tightly in the tapering hole; the Hare cantered round and pelted her with stones and bad names, and she, unable to free herself, shortly afterwards starved to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sheep, the Lamb, the Wolf and the Hare

region.en: Migration road between the southern valley and the great northern plateau (symbolic pin in northern Tibet)
region.zh: 藏南谷地與藏北大高原之間的轉場路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story X

summary.en: A Sheep and her Lamb, met by a Wolf on the road north, bargain for autumn; returning fat, they face the appointment in despair until a Hare rigs the scene - himself in fine robes with an ear-ring and a hat, pen behind his ear, mounted on the saddled Sheep with two bundles lashed on the Lamb. Hailing the Wolf in a sharp official tone as Lomden the Hare, deputed on a special mission by the Emperor of China with a commission of ten wolf-skins for the King of India, he writes a large figure 1 on his sheet of paper - and the Wolf flees ignominiously.
summary.zh: 母羊帶羔北遷遇狼，以「秋天再肥」訂約；歸來時兩代皆肥，赴約在即，兔挺身相救——自己穿上新袍、戴長耳環與時髦帽、耳後別筆，騎上被備鞍的母羊，並在羊羔身上縛好兩個小包袱。臨近狼時他以官腔喝問，自稱「奉中國皇帝特命出使印度的兔子羅木丹，正要向印度王進貢十張狼皮」，隨即在公文上寫下一個大大的「1」字——狼嚇得掉頭狂逃。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; the original collector notes this tale satirizes the arrogance of Tibetan and Chinese officials and the timidity of Tibetan peasants; treated respectfully as social satire of the period.

passages.text: The Hare dressed himself in his best clothes, a new robe of woollen cloth with a long ear-ring in his left ear and a fashionable hat, strapped a small saddle on the Sheep's back, prepared two bundles slung across the Lamb, took a large sheet of paper with a pen thrust behind his ear, and mounted. Soon after, at the appointed spot, the Wolf was waiting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Called out to in a sharp tone of authority, the Wolf replied that he had come to eat the Sheep and its Lamb in accordance with a regular arrangement; the Hare answered that he was Lomden the Hare, deputed to India on a special mission by the Emperor of China, with a commission to bring ten wolf-skins as a present to the King of India - what a fortunate thing it is that I should have met you here; your skin will do for one, anyway. Producing his sheet of paper, he wrote down the figure 1 very large, and the Wolf, so frightened, turned tail and fled away ignominiously.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Hare Made a Fool of the Wolf

region.en: Wolf's earth on a high pass (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 高口埡口的狼穴（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XI

summary.en: Elated by the Hare's rescue, the Sheep and Goat camp at the mouth of the Wolf's earth, sharpening knives and collecting water to cook him in, until the Wolf bolts at the Sheep's nervous voice and kills her. The Goat flees, breaks his leg in a rock cleft, and dies promising his skin to the Fox for his young ones. The Fox meets the Hare, and together they lure the Wolf - found on a dead horse - to a wedding feast; each carries off provisions, and the Wolf, head through the handle of the wine jar, is made to sing before leaving: the men burst in, the jar is too broad for the window, and the Wolf is beaten to death with sticks and stones.
summary.zh: 羊與山羊自恃兔計得逞，蹲在狼穴口磨刀、備水「煮你」，狼卻聽出母羊聲音發抖，撲出將其咬死；山羊逃命跌斷腿，臨終託狐把皮送給孩子。狐遇兔，同往報仇：在喜宴人家偷吃飽喝，兔提議各自帶走食物——羊酪、冷雞、酒罈；狼把頭伸進罈柄，臨走兔又慫恿唱歌，屋內人一聽「屋裡有狼！」一擁而入，罈口太寬塞不過窗，狼被亂棒亂石打死。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Goat rubbed his horns on a stone - sharpening a knife to kill you with - and when rain fell answered that he was collecting the water to cook the Wolf in; but when the nervous Sheep took over the watch, the Wolf noticed the terrified sound of her voice, learned she was alone, dashed out, and slew her. Chasing the fleeing Goat, he lost him in rocky ground, where the Goat fell into a deep narrow cleft and broke his leg; the Wolf jumped over the crevice without seeing him, and the Goat died there, begging the passing Fox to strip off his skin for his young ones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Hare, hearing the Fox's errand, resolved not to let the Wolf kill his friends with impunity, and together they found him feeding on a dead horse and lured him to a wedding feast; through a narrow window they reached the unguarded larder and ate and drank their fill. The Hare advised each to carry off provisions - cheese for himself, cold fowl for the Fox, and the jar of wine for the Wolf, whose head he showed him how to slip through the handle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: As they were about to start the Hare proposed a song, and pressed the modest Wolf until he began to sing; at the first sound of his voice the men in the next room stopped their feasting, crying there is a Wolf in the house, and rushed towards the larder. The Hare and the Fox hopped quietly out of the window; the Wolf made a leap, but the great jar round his neck was too broad for the narrow opening, and he fell back - and was still jumping and falling when the people of the house rushed in and despatched him with sticks and stones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
